input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Describe how we build the document/section graph, represent section dependencies (parent/child, precedence, citation links), and compute a leaf-first writing schedule that prioritizes independent/evidence-ready leaves. Include scheduling heuristics and how the graph is updated during iteration.

output:
We represent a document as a directed acyclic section graph whose nodes correspond to individual manuscript sections (e.g., Introduction subsections, Methods subparts, Results components) and whose edges encode explicit authoring dependencies between sections. Each node stores a small, machine-readable provenance record and a set of runtime attributes that guide generation: a short section spec (title, target length, required fields per the JSON schema), an evidence pool pointer (identifiers for retrieved documents or snippets), an evidence-readiness score, and a completion status (empty / in‑progress / validated). Edges are typed to capture different dependency semantics: parent–child (structural containment), precedence (temporal or logical ordering constraints), and citation links (explicit expected cross-references where a child depends on evidence or claims originating in another node). This typed representation permits downstream scheduling policies to treat distinct dependency kinds differently when deciding generation order.

We build the initial section graph from a high-level document plan (template or user outline). Structural parent–child edges are created from nesting in the outline; precedence edges are added when the outline or author specifies that content in one section must precede or inform another (for example, Methods before Results); and citation-link edges are derived from author-specified cross‑citations or from initial retrieval results that associate particular evidence items with multiple sections. The graph is validated for basic consistency (no self-loops, reachable main root); simple cycles introduced by author error are detected and flagged for human resolution or for automatic breaking via priority heuristics described below.

Scheduling proceeds in a leaf-first, evidence-prioritized fashion. Intuitively, leaves — nodes that have no unresolved child dependencies — are the most independent units and are therefore written first to maximize the use of directly retrieved evidence and to minimize propagation of unsupported claims upward in the document hierarchy. Concretely, the scheduler repeats the following loop until all nodes are completed: (1) identify the current frontier F of eligible nodes (nodes whose child dependencies are all completed and whose precedence constraints are satisfied), (2) compute a priority score for each node in F that combines evidence-readiness, estimated token/effort cost, and author-specified urgency, (3) select one or more top-ranked nodes for generation (single-threaded or batched), (4) generate the node using the evidence-aware prompt and JSON constraints, and (5) validate and integrate the node output, updating the graph state and provenance records.

Priority scoring is implemented as a lightweight, configurable function that balances three design objectives: maximize immediate use of high-quality evidence, reduce propagation of uncertain content into dependent sections, and maintain throughput under compute and token budgets. In our implementation the scheduler ranks frontier nodes by descending evidence-readiness (a scalar reflecting retrieval score aggregates and provenance coverage), penalizes nodes with large estimated generation cost when resources are constrained, and breaks ties using structural depth or author urgency. These components are deliberately modular so practitioners can substitute alternative evidence-scoring heuristics or introduce manual overrides.

Graph updates during iteration are minimal and explicit. After a node is generated, the system (a) marks the node complete and attaches the JSON output and its provenance record (mapping claims to evidence identifiers), (b) reconciles citation links by mapping inline citation placeholders to canonical bib entries or by flagging unresolved citations for re-retrieval, (c) propagates any newly discovered evidence associations to neighboring nodes (for example, if a generated Results subsection cites a dataset paper, that paper is added to the evidence pools of Discussion nodes that depend on interpretation of the results), and (d) recomputes evidence-readiness scores for affected frontier nodes. This incremental update strategy keeps the scheduling decisions tightly coupled to the latest retrieval and generation artifacts and maintains an auditable trail of which evidence supported each claim.

The scheduler includes pragmatic failure-handling heuristics. If no frontier node is evidence-ready above a configurable threshold, the system (i) attempts targeted re-retrieval using section-specific queries augmented with keywords from already-completed neighbors, (ii) relaxes evidence thresholds for low-importance or author-flagged sections with explicit human approval, or (iii) surfaces the stall to a human editor for intervention. Cycle detection reports cycles as explicit authoring errors and offers two resolution policies: prefer precedence edges over citation links, or solicit a user-specified edge removal. For nodes whose generated JSON fails schema validation, the system can attempt a bounded number of automated repair attempts (e.g., re-run generation with stricter evidence injection or ask the model to populate missing required fields), after which the node is escalated for manual correction.

Operationally, the graph representation supports batching and parallelization when resource constraints and dependency structure permit: independent frontier nodes can be generated in parallel provided their evidence pools do not contend for limited retrieval budget and provided downstream deterministic assembly rules exist for integrating concurrent outputs. The graph also supports caching of retrieval results and re-use of evidence snippets across sibling or parent nodes, with provenance pointers preserved so that audits can trace each factual assertion back to its source.

We emphasize that the leaf-first, evidence-prioritized scheduling described here is a design choice intended to improve local factual support and simplify audits; its empirical impact on global coherence and citation fidelity is evaluated in Section 5. Limitations of this construction (notably sensitivity to retrieval coverage and the need for human resolution of ambiguous dependencies) are discussed in Section 6.
